approach: Check whether the friction needed to move both blocks together stays within the maximum available friction; find when it is exceeded, then treat each block separately after that.

steps.text: While the blocks move together, both share the same acceleration from the total applied force.
The friction needed to accelerate block B at this common rate must not exceed the maximum available friction between A and B.
steps.equation: f(needed) = mB × a(common) = 4t/3; f(max) = μmAg = 0.5×2×10 = 10 N

steps.text: Find the time when the needed friction reaches the maximum, which is when the blocks start to slip on each other.
For t < 7.5 s, both blocks move together, reaching 2.5 m/s² at t = 7.5 s.
For t > 7.5 s, friction on B stays fixed at its maximum, so B's acceleration is constant while A speeds up under the growing force minus this fixed friction.

final_answer.value: For 0 ≤ t ≤ 7.5 s, a_A = a_B = t/3, both rising together from 0 to 2.5 m/s². For t > 7.5 s, a_B stays constant at 2.5 m/s², while a_A = t − 5 rises from 2.5 m/s² with slope 1 m/s² per second and is greater than a_B.

common_mistakes.text: Assuming the blocks move together for all time without checking the friction limit gives a_A = a_B = t/3 throughout, missing the point where they slip.
Using the combined weight of both blocks instead of only block A's weight for the maximum friction gives f(max) = 30 N and a much later, wrong slip time of 22.5 s.
